video_title: Why a $1M Startup Wasn’t Worth Building in the Age of AI
gist: a16z's Alex Rampell interviews Town founder/CEO Jean Denis (ex-Plaid CTO) on killing a ~$1M-revenue AI SMB tax startup because it wasn't venture scale post-AI and incumbents would win, then pivoting to an email/calendar AI assistant. They discuss PLG-first strategy, competing with AI labs via model neutrality and data ownership, AI diffusion being bottlenecked by 'tinkerers', and agents breaking the ad-supported covenant for aggregators like Amazon.

themes.theme: Killing a sub-venture AI tax startup

insights.claim: Town originally automated SMB business tax returns and reached a little under $1M revenue in year one with a plan for $2.5-3M in year two, which the founder judged a good pre-AI business but not venture scale post-AI.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Post-AI, VC bar for growth rates has risen: ~3x year-two growth off $1M is no longer considered venture scale.
insights.quote: But post-AI, it just it just this was not going to be a venture scale company.

insights.claim: The founder concluded that tax-prep incumbents would use AI to automate prep for their existing customers faster than a new entrant could grab market share, because incumbents hold distribution advantages.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: In AI-automatable verticals with entrenched distribution, incumbents may capture the AI upside; discount startups lacking a distribution wedge.
insights.quote: the incumbents were going to be able to use the technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than we could grab market share

insights.claim: New entrants face a 'ticking clock': they must achieve word-of-mouth network effects and market penetration before incumbents copy the product effectively.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Assess AI startups on speed to penetration relative to incumbent copy speed, not just product quality.
insights.quote: there's a ticking clock on the wall

insights.claim: Annual-purchase categories like tax (and EdTech, which sells only twice a year to schools) cannot hyper-scale because they lack daily usage and word-of-mouth occurs out of sync with buying windows.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Seasonal/once-a-year purchase cadence is a structural growth cap; avoid underwriting hypergrowth in such categories.
insights.quote: Those discontinuity make it really difficult to to hyper scale.

insights.claim: Because tax is cyclical, Town had only about a one-month window around October 15 to pivot before committing to customers for the next season, and that time pressure forced a faster decision than a continuous business would.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Cyclical businesses impose hard decision deadlines that can make pivots cleaner.

insights.claim: The founder framed the pivot around team opportunity cost: if leadership stops believing in a great outcome, it is hard to recruit against candidates' liquid offers elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Talent competition from liquid incumbents raises the bar for founders continuing middling startups.

insights.claim: Town pivoted after tax customers kept asking for help with meetings, meeting prep and drafting answers to recurring client questions, revealing that no one had built great AI around common email-and-calendar knowledge-worker workflows.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Adjacent customer requests in a failing product can reveal a larger horizontal market.
insights.quote: no one had built great AI around these very common knowledge worker workflows like meetings, meeting prep, meeting outcome

insights.claim: Town found product-market fit very quickly as models became more agentic around the Opus 4.5 era, growing roughly 1-1.5% per day from December to April in closed beta.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Model capability step-changes can create sudden PMF windows; ~1%+ daily growth compounds to multiples in months.
insights.quote: Like every day the product grew by a percent or a percent and a half.

insights.claim: Town sees a large global TAM because most businesses, especially external-facing roles like sales, BD and recruiting, run out of email and calendar.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Email/calendar agents address a horizontal, worldwide market rather than a niche.

insights.claim: AI personal assistants as a category are used by only a few million people worldwide, and the founder expects 6-18 months before most people experience the magic even in their personal lives.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Assistant category is early on the adoption curve; significant runway for growth.
insights.quote: assistance as a category is used by a few million folks, right? Worldwide today.

insights.claim: The host argues AI assistants exhibit a Jevons paradox: the executive-assistant market looks small because few people have one, but producing an assistant via silicon expands demand massively, including tasks like reading all email that no one would give a human.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Cheap AI labor expands addressable markets far beyond the size of the human-labor market it replaces.
insights.quote: if you could actually produce it via silicon, the market's quite large, and then you find things to do

insights.claim: Town describes its product as a 'token allocation machine' that suggests places a user could apply AI tokens, letting the human choose which outcomes they want.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: As token costs fall, the value accrues to products that surface new uses for tokens.
insights.quote: I think of our of our product as a token allocation machine.

insights.claim: As tokens get cheaper, long-tail tasks like writing research-backed prep notes for every meeting become worth doing at roughly a penny each, whereas even an executive assistant would never do them.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Falling inference costs unlock long-tail automation demand that never existed with human labor.

insights.claim: A restaurant owner can prompt Town in about 5 minutes to monthly compare wholesaler price sheets; it costs about $1/month and in the one month a year it finds something it can surface hundreds or thousands of dollars in savings.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: SMB ROI cases for agents are concrete and lopsided, supporting PLG adoption among small businesses.
insights.quote: it's going to cost you like a dollar a month to run that thing

insights.claim: The host argues SMBs will not buy an 'executive assistant' but will buy concrete savings, like saving $500 a year on iceberg lettuce for $52 a year, framing AI adoption as a product-marketing problem.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Agent products sell on specific outcomes, not abstract capability; marketing framing drives SMB adoption.

insights.claim: Town's stickiness signal is a user connecting email, calendar, one important system of record, and building one custom integration; the company aims to eliminate the need for the custom integration step.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Activation metrics for agent products center on system-of-record connections and one 'magic' custom workflow.
insights.quote: They've connected their email, their calendar and ideally one really important system of record for their business.

insights.claim: Drawing on Dropbox experience, Town's founders believe it is possible to take a world-class consumer-grade product into the enterprise but almost impossible to start from compliance/IT requirements and then make the product great.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Favor AI apps that start user-first/PLG; enterprise-first builds risk poor product quality when buyer and user differ.
insights.quote: It is almost impossible to go from an experience that starts from the compliance IT enterprise requirements

insights.claim: Town's thesis is that CIOs and CEOs will demand at work the consumer-grade personal-assistant experience they get personally, so whoever delivers enterprise software that feels like consumer software will win.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Consumerization of enterprise AI favors consumer-grade apps over IT-led incumbents.
insights.quote: whoever has an enterprise experience that feels like a consumer experience, like they're going to be set up to win

insights.claim: The host compares the moment to the iPhone killing BlackBerry after CEOs got iPhones personally and ordered IT to make them work, despite Steve Ballmer's dismissal of an $800 phone.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Bottom-up executive adoption can collapse enterprise incumbents quickly.

insights.claim: The founder warns the risk is not only being BlackBerry but being Good Technologies: an enterprise-ready iPhone email client that failed because it lacked the quality of other iPhone apps.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Enterprise-compliant wrappers lose to native consumer-quality products; security alone is not a moat.

insights.claim: Agents become more effective with access to a company's data and APIs, so Town's adoption path is to earn trust via email/calendar first and only later ask for CRM and other system connections, a journey that moves at human speed in large enterprises.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Enterprise agent adoption is gated by data access and trust; expect slower ramps in Fortune 100 than in SMB.

insights.claim: Enterprise AI requires audit logs, privileged-information controls and CFO cost controls over token spend; Town focuses product and self-serve growth on SMB/mid-market while building security, compliance and finance features for enterprise.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Token cost governance is an emerging enterprise buying requirement for AI tools.

insights.claim: The founder argues AI product capabilities will converge across harnesses, making feature leads hard to sustain, and that the unit of software value has shifted from the app to the computer, so value will drop in the app layer.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Feature-based differentiation in AI apps is fragile; app-layer margins may compress.
insights.quote: I think the value will drop in the app layer.

insights.claim: Town's differentiation bet is AI-driven per-user customization: it interviews power users by vertical (e.g., 10 restaurant owners), builds template 'routines', and matches new signups to them, aiming at 80/20 custom software for each person.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Scalable AI personalization via a learning flywheel is pitched as the moat versus generic harnesses.

insights.claim: Town scales customer research with AI-recorded interviews incentivized with Amazon gift cards, so the routine library improves at the speed of AI rather than humans.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: AI-native companies can automate product discovery itself, compounding learning speed.

insights.claim: The founder predicts the labs' forward-deployed-engineer (FDE) approach, e.g., enterprises paying OpenAI ~$5M a year for FDEs, looks good now but gets much worse as models improve, while automated custom-software approaches scale better.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Bearish on human-services-heavy enterprise AI deployment models; bullish on automated personalization.
insights.quote: if you're a enterprise that's willing to spend like 5 million a year paying OpenAI for FDEs, like, it looks really good right now

insights.claim: Town pitches model neutrality: mid-market firms (500-1,000 employees) cannot know which model provider will be best over 3-5 years, so a neutral app routing to the best supplier per task (voice, video, slides) de-risks vendor choice.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Neutral multi-model app layers have a durable pitch as long as frontier leadership rotates.
insights.quote: We will use whatever supplier we think is the best for you in the moment.

insights.claim: Companies that standardized on OpenAI two years ago had to also adopt Anthropic's Claude when it led in coding for about 12 months, showing the cost of single-provider lock-in.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Model leadership rotates; enterprises are likely to multi-source, benefiting routers and hurting exclusive lab platforms.

insights.claim: Town's second pitch is data ownership: businesses should fully own their AI context and memories so switching to a better solution takes a day, while FDE-built software is designed to increase switching costs.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: 'Context' is a new business asset; portability vs lock-in is a key battleground between apps and labs.
insights.quote: switching to that other solution would take you know, a day

insights.claim: The founder warns that if a company's operating know-how ends up in a model's weights that is resold, it effectively sells what makes the business successful to others; Town does not train on customer data.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Training-data concerns support demand for non-training, neutral AI vendors.

insights.claim: The founder cites OpenAI building vertical products competing with Rogo and Harvey as evidence that labs move up the stack, arguing large companies should not be beholden to any one lab's app.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Vertical AI apps face direct lab competition; neutrality becomes a strategic selling point.

insights.claim: The host argues a 'Goldilocks zone' of relevance protects horizontal apps: coding is so large for Anthropic that labs cannot ignore it, while spread-out horizontal assistant use cases are harder for labs to commit to; he notes OpenAI learned focus after Anthropic went all-in on code.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Startups are safest in markets material enough to be large but not yet core to lab revenue.

insights.claim: The founder counters that AI for running businesses is a bigger market than coding and predicts it will move the needle at the labs within about 12 months, making lab competition a question of when, not if.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect frontier labs to target horizontal work assistants within ~a year, pressuring startups in that space.
insights.quote: for me it's a question of like when not if

insights.claim: Town's Teams product lets agents of different employees talk to each other to answer questions like who knows someone at a prospect, trusting AI to mediate privacy instead of humans reading Slack messages and answering a day later.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent internal routing could displace human coordination layers in collaboration tools.
insights.quote: Humans are slow routers.

insights.claim: The founder believes the future involves far less human in the loop and that the economic benefit to companies far outstrips the risks.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Products designed for autonomous agent workflows may outpace human-in-the-loop designs.
insights.quote: the future looks like a lot less human in the loop than we see today

insights.claim: The founder argues AI is not diffusing because few businesses have 'tinkerers' to build solutions; features in Claude and ChatGPT that could save small businesses time have existed for 12 months but are used as a better Google search.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: The AI adoption gap is product/deployment, not intelligence; winners will package value for non-tinkerers.
insights.quote: the product experience can't just be a text box

insights.claim: The founder says the intelligence already exists and the real unlock is deploying it effectively at scale; whoever makes a non-tinkerer get a tinkerer's value could be a ginormous business today.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Distribution and onboarding layers on top of existing models are a large near-term opportunity.
insights.quote: you don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there.

insights.claim: The host argues Silicon Valley may overhype AI while the rest of the world underhypes it, partly because early adopters tried AI two years ago, saw hallucinations, and ossified that view.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Large latent demand exists outside tech as perceptions catch up with capability.

insights.claim: Computer and browser use improved sharply in the last ~2.5 months: assistants now complete tasks about 90% of the time that they managed only ~30% of the time six months ago.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Rapid reliability gains in computer-use agents expand automatable workflows quickly.
insights.quote: they can do them 90% of the time whereas before they were doing it like 30% of the time

insights.claim: The founder says Town is unexpectedly popular in odd niches and geographies (e.g., big in Japan, a surfboard rental business using it to inspect damage photos for deposit decisions), driven by tinkerers rather than targeted marketing.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Horizontal PLG agents surface unforeseen vertical use cases worldwide.

insights.claim: The host claims agent traffic has vastly surpassed human traffic on the internet and that the ad covenant of free content in exchange for eyeballs is broken by agents.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Ad-supported publishers and aggregators face monetization erosion from agent traffic.

insights.claim: The founder argues Amazon's adversarial stance toward agents should be Walmart's gain, since Walmart lacks a large advertising business to protect.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Retailers without ad businesses may win agent-driven commerce share from Amazon.
insights.quote: Amazon's loss should be Walmart's gain

insights.claim: The founder favors neutral agents whose only revenue source is the user's wallet, warning that an ad-funded agent (e.g., Meta's, with airline advertisers) would lose user trust in its recommendations.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Ad-funded agent models face trust headwinds; subscription-funded neutral agents may win.

insights.claim: The founder distinguishes friction humans enjoy (browsing shops in SoHo, discovering toys with ads) from friction they do not (reordering toilet paper), arguing ad-driven aggregators will still have value for the former.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Agent disruption hits replenishment commerce hardest; discovery/entertainment commerce stays ad-monetizable.

insights.claim: The founder argues Amazon should not block agents since a 'headless Amazon' could be bigger than Amazon, and that Amazon risks losing a large chunk of its roughly $70-80B ad business fighting the future; its countermove should be its own personal agent bundled into Prime.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Amazon's ad revenue is exposed to agentic shopping; watch for an Amazon personal agent strategy.
insights.quote: a headless Amazon could be a huge huge business

insights.claim: The founder suggests Meta's free Muse agent may never need ads, instead feeding data to better target Instagram ads and payments, divorcing monetization from the agent experience.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Meta may monetize personal agents indirectly through its ad network, an advantage over pure aggregators.

insights.claim: The host cites CamelCamelCamel, an 18-year-old Amazon price-tracking affiliate site used by about 20 million Americans, as evidence that agents will give money-rich, time-poor people the deal-hunting behaviors of time-rich people.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Price discrimination schemes (coupons, card perks) relying on time cost will erode as agents automate them.

insights.claim: Agents optimizing coupons and Amex/Chase premium card benefits will break price-discrimination covenants and force issuers to change programs.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z)
insights.so_what: Card rewards economics and coupon-based marketing are at risk from agent optimization.

insights.claim: The founder's through-line is that supply aggregation is far less valuable than before because it relied on limited human attention, which can now be automated away.
insights.speaker: Jean Denis (Town CEO)
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for aggregator business models (marketplaces, ad-funded aggregators) in an agentic world.
insights.quote: supply aggregation is a lot less valuable because human attention can be automated away
